cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: FANCG is a TPR-domain scaffold protein essential for the Fanconi anemia (FA) DNA interstrand crosslink repair pathway, where it nucleates assembly of both the FA nuclear core complex and a distinct D1-D2-G-X3 complex to promote genome integrity. Through its seven TPR motifs, FANCG directly binds FANCA (stabilizing its protein levels and driving nuclear accumulation of the core complex), FANCC, BRCA2/FANCD1, and XRCC3, thereby enabling monoubiquitination of FANCD2 and efficient homologous recombination repair [PMID:10373536, PMID:14697762, PMID:12861027, PMID:16621732]. Phosphorylation of FANCG at serine 7 is required for assembly of the core-complex-independent D1-D2-G-X3 sub-complex, while CDK1-mediated phosphorylation at serines 383/387 during mitosis and K63-linked polyubiquitination at K182/K258/K347 are each independently required for full pathway function and interaction with the Rap80–BRCA1 complex [PMID:15299017, PMID:15367677, PMID:25132264]. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in FANCG cause Fanconi anemia complementation group G, characterized by cellular hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, chromosomal instability, and impaired fertility [PMID:9806548, PMID:11719385].

GCLC encodes the catalytic subunit of glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL), which catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of glutathione (GSH) biosynthesis and is essential for embryonic viability, hepatic and neuronal mitochondrial integrity, and protection against ferroptosis [PMID:11118286, PMID:17464988, PMID:28158580, PMID:40188196]. GCLC transcription is activated primarily through the Nrf2/Keap1–ARE axis downstream of ERK, p38, JNK, and NADPH oxidase-derived ROS signaling, and is also regulated by Nrf1–small Maf heterodimers, while USF1/2-mediated E-box binding and promoter hypermethylation serve as repressive mechanisms [PMID:11097862, PMID:14500406, PMID:11342101, PMID:16198230, PMID:26087411]. Post-translationally, GCLC is activated by SIRT2-mediated desuccinylation at K38/K126/K326 (opposing P300-catalyzed succinylation), and its catalytic output declines with age through cleavage at D499, generating truncated fragments that compete with full-length GCLC for GCLM heterodimerization [PMID:40188196, PMID:38669339]. GCLC mRNA stability is further enhanced by NSUN2-mediated m5C methylation, and its translation is promoted by SNORA56-dependent pseudouridylation of 28S rRNA, both of which sustain GSH levels and suppress ferroptosis [PMID:39742570, PMID:38049865].

LIG1 is the principal replicative DNA ligase in human cells, sealing Okazaki fragments during lagging-strand synthesis and completing nick ligation in base excision repair (BER) and ribonucleotide excision repair pathways. It catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation through a three-step AMP-dependent mechanism, using two PCNA-interacting motifs to assemble a toolbelt complex with PCNA and FEN1 on nicked DNA—where PIPN-term mediates initial recruitment and PIPDBD sustains ligation, enabling substrate handoff from FEN1 [PMID:36539424]—while its N-terminal non-catalytic domain drives one-dimensional diffusion along DNA to locate nick sites [PMID:39404052]. LIG1 discriminates against aberrant substrates through active-site residues F635 and F872 that enforce DNA end rigidity to block mismatch ligation [PMID:39574773], a cooperative network coupling DNA engagement to Mg²⁺ cofactor binding [PMID:33444456], and asymmetric sugar selectivity that permits 3′-ribonucleotide but rejects 5′-ribonucleotide nick sealing [PMID:38522520, PMID:39159820]; APE1 acts as a compensatory proofreader removing mismatched or damaged 3′-ends that escape this fidelity checkpoint [PMID:35790757, PMID:38366780]. LIG1 catalytic activity is selectively essential in BRCA1-deficient cells, where its loss causes accumulation of single-strand breaks, replication stress, and synthetic lethality both in vitro and in vivo [PMID:39868490, PMID:39718835], and the Huntington's disease-modifier variant K845N enhances mismatch discrimination and suppresses somatic CAG repeat expansion in HD knock-in mice [PMID:41770933].

UCHL5 (UCH37) is a deubiquitinase of the ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase family that functions as a proteasome-associated chain editor and a regulator of multiple signaling pathways. At the 26S proteasome, UCHL5 is recruited via its C-terminal extension binding RPN13/ADRM1, which relieves autoinhibition caused by UCHL5 oligomerization and activates processive exo-cleavage and debranching of K48-linked polyubiquitin chains, thereby facilitating substrate degradation [PMID:16906146, PMID:24752541, PMID:33156996]. UCHL5 also associates with the hINO80 chromatin-remodeling complex through NFRKB/INO80G, which holds the enzyme catalytically inactive via molecular mimicry that blocks the ubiquitin-binding site, and crystal structures demonstrate that the opposing DEUBAD domains of RPN13 and NFRKB exploit the same structural elements to achieve activation versus inhibition [PMID:18922472, PMID:25702870, PMID:25702872]. Beyond the proteasome, UCHL5 deubiquitinates non-proteasomal substrates including the TGF-β type I receptor/ALK5, E2F1 (K63-linked chains), Smoothened, NLRP3, and Axin1, modulating TGF-β, Hedgehog, Wnt/β-catenin, and inflammasome signaling, and its deletion in mice causes prenatal lethality with severe brain defects [PMID:16027725, PMID:26396186, PMID:28992318, PMID:34431717, PMID:35256667, PMID:21048919].

CCNL2 (Cyclin L2) is a nuclear RS-domain-containing cyclin that localizes to nuclear speckles and functions as an activating partner of CDK11, coupling cyclin-dependent kinase activity to pre-mRNA splicing and alternative splice-site selection [PMID:14623875, PMID:18216018]. Cyclin L2 directly interacts with SR-family splicing factors, and ectopic expression of its full-length isoforms enhances in vitro splicing activity, whereas CDK11 kinase-dead mutants repress splicing [PMID:18216018]. CCNL2 is itself subject to multi-layered regulation: DYRK1A phosphorylates it, miR-214 represses its translation, KLF3 transcriptionally activates its gene, YBX1 stabilizes its mRNA via m5C modification, and CLK1/SRSF5-driven aberrant exon skipping generates a truncated isoform that promotes cancer-cell proliferation [PMID:14623875, PMID:27381447, PMID:34937039, PMID:40707993, PMID:33849617]. Aberrant splicing or loss of full-length CCNL2 is linked to enhanced proliferation in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and ovarian cancer, and its genomic co-deletion with CDK11 at 1p36 creates a therapeutic vulnerability to CDK11 inhibition [PMID:33849617, PMID:40707993].

CLPX is a AAA+ ATPase unfoldase that forms asymmetric hexameric rings and uses ATP hydrolysis to mechanically grip, unfold, and translocate polypeptide substrates through conserved aromatic pore-loop residues into the ClpP peptidase chamber for degradation, with substrate selectivity determined by five classes of recognition motifs and modulated by adaptor proteins such as SspB and RssB that dock to the N-terminal zinc-binding domain (ZBD) [PMID:8226770, PMID:12667450, PMID:14536077, PMID:18931677]. Independent of ClpP and ATP hydrolysis, CLPX functions as a molecular chaperone that remodels stable protein complexes—disassembling MuA transpososomes by partial unfolding of individual subunits, activating the TrfA replication initiator by monomerization, and inhibiting FtsZ polymerization—demonstrating broad protease-independent remodeling activity [PMID:7557391, PMID:11545746, PMID:9405620, PMID:15948963]. In the mitochondrial matrix, CLPX activates 5-aminolevulinate synthase (ALAS) by catalyzing partial unfolding that gates pyridoxal phosphate cofactor incorporation, thereby controlling the committed step of heme biosynthesis; CLPX also regulates ALAS turnover, PPOX activity, and ferrochelatase levels during erythroid differentiation [PMID:25957689, PMID:32091391, PMID:34280433]. A dominant loss-of-function mutation (p.Gly298Asp) in the CLPX ATPase active site causes ALAS accumulation and protoporphyrin IX excess, resulting in erythropoietic protoporphyria [PMID:28874591].

EAPP is a nuclear phosphoprotein that functions as a transcriptional regulator at the intersection of cell proliferation and apoptosis control. It physically interacts with activating E2F family members (E2F-1, -2, -3) to stimulate E2F-dependent transcription and S-phase entry, while independently binding the p21 promoter to activate p21 expression in a p53-independent manner, thereby promoting G1 arrest and resistance to DNA damage-induced apoptosis [PMID:15716352, PMID:21258403]. EAPP also competes with Sp1 at GC-box elements to repress MAO B transcription, activates the MDR1 promoter through an E2F1-independent mechanism, and modulates checkpoint kinase Chk2 activity by promoting its dephosphorylation [PMID:20980443, PMID:23542036, PMID:21572256]. EAPP levels are frequently elevated in transformed cells, in part due to reduced Sp3-mediated repression of its TATA-less promoter, and its abundance in aneuploid tumor cells is consistent with its role in attenuating Chk2-dependent genome surveillance [PMID:18588995, PMID:21572256].

FBXW9 is an F-box/WD40-repeat substrate-recognition subunit of SCF (SKP1–CUL1–F-box) ubiquitin ligase complexes that targets proteins for proteasomal degradation to promote neuronal differentiation, microtubule formation, and synaptic vesicle trafficking [PMID:15520277, PMID:32467239]. Studies of its C. elegans ortholog MEC-15 demonstrate that the SCF^FBXW9 complex ubiquitinates and degrades DLK-1, a MAP3K and Hsp90 client, with opposing regulation by the Hsp70/Hsp90 chaperone machinery and the phosphatase PPP5C [PMID:32467239, PMID:35361529]. MEC-15 is required specifically for GABAergic synaptic transmission, where it controls synaptic vesicle protein localization [PMID:23527112]. In mammalian cells, FBXW9 knockdown stabilizes p21 and arrests cell cycle progression, consistent with a role in degrading TP53-pathway components [PMID:36982338].

HNRNPUL2 is a heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein that directly binds mRNA and participates in the DNA double-strand break (DSB) response. It is recruited to DNA damage sites in an MRN (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1)-dependent manner, where it stimulates DNA-end resection, promotes ATR signaling and homologous recombination repair, and facilitates BLM helicase recruitment downstream of MRN and CtIP, functioning interdependently with its paralog hnRNPUL1 [PMID:22365830]. HNRNPUL2 is a bona fide mRNA-binding protein identified by UV-crosslinking interactome capture in multiple cell types [PMID:22658674, PMID:22681889], and it forms a functional complex with the lncRNA CRNDE, whose binding directs hnRNPUL2 nucleocytoplasmic shuttling and reciprocally stabilizes the lncRNA [PMID:28594403].

KDM8 (JMJD5) is a 2-oxoglutarate- and Fe(II)-dependent JmjC oxygenase that functions principally as a stereoselective arginyl C-3 hydroxylase on protein substrates (RCCD1, RPS6, ISY1, NFATc1) and as a histone tail endopeptidase that clips methylarginine- and monomethyllysine-containing N-terminal tails of H3 and other histones, activities that collectively regulate chromatin state, transcriptional elongation, cell cycle progression, and genome integrity [PMID:29563586, PMID:28847961, PMID:28982940]. Through its hydroxylase activity KDM8 modulates the p53–CDKN1A axis and cyclin A1 expression to control G1/S progression — Jmjd5 knockout mice die at midgestation with p53/p21 hyperactivation, rescued by Cdkn1a or Trp53 co-deletion — and couples with CDK9-phosphorylated RNA Pol II to clip +1 nucleosome tails for transcriptional pause release [PMID:22241836, PMID:26334721, PMID:32747552]. KDM8 additionally reprograms glucose metabolism by binding PKM2 to block its tetramerization and promote nuclear PKM2/HIF-1α co-activation of glycolytic genes, tunes circadian period by facilitating FBXL3-dependent proteasomal degradation of CRY1, maintains mitochondrial gene networks in cardiomyocytes by repressing TBX15 through H3K36me2 demethylation, and influences DNA double-strand break repair pathway choice via interaction with RAD51 [PMID:24344305, PMID:30500822, PMID:38665902, PMID:42001401]. Loss of Kdm8 in cardiomyocytes initiates dilated cardiomyopathy that is preventable by NAD+ supplementation [PMID:38665902].

PI4KA is a type III phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase that generates the plasma membrane pool of phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P), a lipid essential for PI(4,5)P2 homeostasis during receptor-coupled phospholipase C signaling, phosphatidylserine asymmetry, and KRAS membrane anchorage [PMID:24415756, PMID:34504076]. It functions as a heterotetrameric complex with TTC7, FAM126, and the membrane-anchored adaptor EFR3, whose C-terminus undergoes a disorder-to-order transition upon binding TTC7–FAM126 to recruit PI4KA to the plasma membrane, and is regulated by calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation at the EFR3-binding interface [PMID:39705356, PMID:39216471, PMID:41197736]. Catalytic activity depends on conserved residues Lys-1792 and Asp-1854 within the C-terminal kinase domain [PMID:11311856, PMID:25855803]. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, inflammatory bowel disease, and combined immunodeficiency, while compound heterozygous catalytic-domain mutations cause perisylvian polymicrogyria and cerebellar hypoplasia [PMID:34415310, PMID:25855803].

PNRC2 is a proline-rich adaptor protein that functions as a decapping coactivator and bridges mRNA surveillance factors to the cytoplasmic mRNA decay machinery. Its crystal structure with Dcp1a reveals that the proline-rich region binds the EVH1 domain of Dcp1a while its NR-box motif binds hyperphosphorylated UPF1, enabling PNRC2 to bridge Dcp1a and Dcp2 and stimulate decapping followed by 5′-to-3′ exonucleolytic degradation [PMID:23085078, PMID:29348139]. Through these interactions, PNRC2 mediates glucocorticoid receptor–dependent mRNA decay (GMD) of chemokine transcripts such as CCL2 [PMID:25775514] and Pumilio/ARE-dependent turnover of oscillatory segmentation clock transcripts in zebrafish [PMID:28648842, PMID:32246943]. PNRC2-null mice are lean and resistant to diet-induced obesity with elevated metabolic rates, establishing an in vivo role in energy homeostasis [PMID:17971453].

TECR is the sole mammalian trans-2,3-enoyl-CoA reductase that catalyzes the final NADPH-dependent reduction step of the very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) elongation cycle, converting trans-2,3-enoyl-CoA intermediates to saturated acyl-CoAs [PMID:12482854]. Beyond VLCFA synthesis, TECR functions in the sphingosine 1-phosphate degradation pathway by reducing trans-2-hexadecenoyl-CoA to palmitoyl-CoA, thereby linking sphingolipid catabolism to fatty acid elongation [PMID:25049234]. A homozygous P182L missense mutation causes autosomal recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability, reduces enzymatic activity and protein stability, and depletes C24 sphingomyelin and ceramide species [PMID:21212097, PMID:24220030]. In brain endothelial cells, TECR-dependent production of omega-3 fatty acids suppresses caveolae-mediated transcytosis and is required for blood–brain barrier integrity during development [PMID:35465346].

CIROZ (formerly C1orf127) encodes a secreted protein with a signal peptide and three zona pellucida N domains that is specifically expressed in the vertebrate left-right organizer (LRO), where it functions as an essential component of embryonic left-right symmetry breaking in mammals [PMID:39753129]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in CIROZ cause heterotaxy with congenital heart defects in humans, and Ciroz knockout mice display situs anomalies, establishing it as a bona fide laterality gene [PMID:39753129, PMID:40030011]. CIROZ operates within a genetic module that includes DAND5, PKD1L1, MMP21, and CIROP, all co-expressed in the LRO, though its requirement for left-right patterning is not universal across vertebrates, as it is dispensable in zebrafish and Xenopus and has been lost or pseudogenized in certain lineages including Carnivora and jawless vertebrates [PMID:39753129].
